entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John of Worcester, an English Benedictine monk and chronicler active at Worcester Priory, stands as a pivotal figure in the historiography of Anglo-Norman England, primarily through his authorship of the *Chronicon ex Chronicis*. Active in the late 11th and early 12th centuries, with his death recorded around 1200, John meticulously compiled a universal chronicle that offered an unparalleled, continuous narrative of English history from creation to his own time. His work is invaluable for understanding the political, ecclesiastical, and social landscape of England, particularly during the tumultuous decades following the Norman Conquest and the reign of King Stephen.

The *Chronicon ex Chronicis* represents a monumental scholarly endeavor, extending the earlier work of Marianus Scotus and significantly expanding upon it with detailed accounts of English affairs. John systematically integrated various sources, including Anglo-Saxon chronicles, monastic annals, and charters, to construct a coherent, year-by-year record. His chronicle provides critical insights into events such as the Domesday Survey of 1086, the Investiture Controversy in England (1103–1107), and the succession crises of the early 12th century. The original manuscript, now Bodleian Library MS. Laud Misc. 636, showcases his dedication to historical accuracy and comprehensive coverage.
